# The Weight of Water: Community-Governed Quantum Gravimetry for Contested Aquifers

## Project Abstract

Groundwater regulation usually depends on extraction declarations, a small number of instrumented wells, and hydrological models that residents cannot independently examine. In the drought-prone Morrow Delta, this evidence system has become a source of political conflict. Large licensed farms report pumping by quarter, while small leaseholders and households using unregistered wells face restrictions based on estimates. Residents of the low-income East Sill district also report subsidence and building damage, but the regional water authority maintains that it cannot reliably distinguish groundwater loss from soil compaction and construction. These disputes concern more than measurement: they determine whose water use is visible, whose testimony is accepted, and who bears the cost of scarcity.

We propose a 30-month pilot to test whether a network of rubidium-87 atom-interferometric gravimeters can provide an independent, publicly governed measure of groundwater storage change. Cold-atom gravimeters infer local gravitational acceleration from the phase accumulated by freely falling atomic wave packets. Because groundwater adds measurable mass beneath a sensor, repeated observations may reveal storage changes without requiring access to every well. Our central hypothesis is that jointly analysing quantum-gravity observations, well pressure, soil moisture, and land-motion data will identify pumping-related mass changes at a scale useful for neighborhood water-allocation decisions. The project combines quantum metrology, hydrogeology, participatory mapping, and public administration.

**Aim 1: Build and validate a field-ready quantum gravity network.** We will install twelve fixed gravimeter nodes across a nine-by-six-kilometre section of the lower Morrow aquifer, placing instruments at libraries, irrigation offices, schools, and two industrial facilities. Two additional instruments will operate as roving references. Each node will use vibration isolation, barometric correction, and automated laser-frequency checks, with ten-minute measurements aggregated into daily estimates. The target repeatability is 0.5 microgal after daily averaging. Twenty-four borehole pressure loggers, six precipitation stations, four continuous satellite-positioning receivers, and soil-moisture probes will measure major non-groundwater influences. Earth tides, atmospheric loading, instrument drift, and observed vertical motion will be removed through a common processing pipeline. Monthly side-by-side measurements with a calibrated spring gravimeter will test bias and long-term stability. Performance milestones are 80% network uptime, less than 1.5 microgal disagreement between co-located instruments, and detection of an aquifer recharge event independently observed in at least six pressure loggers.

**Aim 2: Estimate where and when groundwater mass changes occur.** We will develop a physics-informed Bayesian inversion that represents the aquifer as 250-metre horizontal cells with three depth layers. Daily gravity estimates will be combined with geological priors and pressure measurements to generate maps of storage change and credible intervals. Pumping declarations will not be used to fit the model; instead, they will be compared with inferred extraction patterns after each quarter. Two large licensed facilities have agreed to planned 48-hour pumping pauses, creating perturbations with known timing. These pauses will test whether the network detects both cessation and recovery. A western sector will be withheld from initial model fitting as a validation area. We will compare the quantum network with a conventional monitoring strategy based only on pressure loggers and reported pumping, evaluating forecast error, detection latency, and the proportion of mapped cells for which uncertainty is narrow enough to support an alert.

**Aim 3: Create a civic evidence protocol rather than a new enforcement instrument.** A Water Evidence Council will include four residents selected by neighborhood assemblies, two small-farm representatives, two industrial users, one water-authority analyst, one hydrologist, and one tenant advocate. During six workshops, the council will define acceptable map resolution, retention periods, and rules for communicating uncertainty. Public outputs will report storage changes by zone rather than identify household wells. An alert will require agreement between gravity and at least one non-gravity data stream, persistence for three days, and posterior probability above 0.9. Alerts will trigger field verification and a public explanation, not an automatic penalty. Raw atomic phase records and exact household-well coordinates will remain restricted because vibration signatures and location data could reveal private activity. Processed gravity series, correction code, uncertainty summaries, and meeting decisions will be released through a locally maintained data repository.

The governance protocol will be tested through three simulated allocation hearings and, if a drought declaration occurs during the project, one live advisory exercise. Participants will receive either existing authority reports or the new multi-sensor evidence package. We will assess comprehension, confidence, perceived procedural fairness, and proposed allocation decisions before and after facilitated discussion. Interviews will examine whether the system changes whose claims are treated as credible. Because small users may lack time or technical expertise to participate, the project will fund childcare, transport, interpretation, and independent technical briefings. The regional authority will not receive household-level products, although it may request temporary access to restricted records during an infrastructure emergency after approval by the project director and council chair.

Success will be defined by five outcomes: sustained field operation at the stated precision; detection of both planned pumping pauses; daily storage maps at 250-metre resolution over at least 70% of the study area; improved one-month groundwater forecasts relative to the conventional network; and evidence that at least two stakeholder groups revise an allocation proposal after reviewing quantified uncertainty. The project will also deliver a modular gravimeter enclosure, an open processing workflow, a model charter for community oversight, and a cost projection for a delta-wide network.

By treating quantum sensing as an institution for producing shared evidence, not merely as a more sensitive instrument, this project addresses a neglected barrier to climate adaptation: measurements can intensify inequality when access and interpretation remain centralized. If successful, the pilot will show how quantum gravimetry can make hidden groundwater loss visible while limiting household surveillance. The resulting approach could be transferred to other drought-affected basins where extraction records are incomplete and trust in water governance is low.
planted_strengths: The abstract identifies a consequential and non-obvious use of quantum sensing: the governance of disputed groundwater extraction and allocation.

The measurement plan is technically concrete, specifying rubidium-87 atom interferometry, instrument numbers, correction methods, comparator sensors, operational milestones, and planned pumping pauses.
The project recognizes that gravity measurements are not self-interpreting and incorporates pressure, soil-moisture, precipitation, positioning, and conventional gravimeter data.

The proposal handles social stakes in good faith through privacy protections, community participation, uncertainty communication, compensation for participation, and a presumption against automatic enforcement.
It includes measurable outputs, a withheld validation sector, an explicit timeline, and a comparison against a conventional monitoring strategy.
planted_weaknesses: The proposed reconstruction of daily groundwater changes in 250-metre cells and three depth layers is implausibly ambitious for twelve fixed gravity sensors because gravity inversion is non-unique and has weak depth resolution.

The abstract gives a precision target but no sensitivity or power analysis showing that expected groundwater signals, after environmental corrections, will exceed noise at the claimed spatial and temporal resolution.

The validation design is limited: two pumping pauses at large facilities may demonstrate detection of known events but cannot establish reliable attribution among multiple simultaneous pumping and recharge sources.

The governance study has no stated sample size, analytic method, or credible strategy for separating the effect of better measurements from facilitation, presentation, or pre-existing stakeholder preferences.

The emergency-access exception is underspecified and concentrates authority in the project director and council chair, weakening the otherwise participatory data-governance framework and creating potential for surveillance mission creep. Housing sensitive records in a project-controlled repository is also not fully justified, although access is restricted and public outputs are aggregated and non-punitive, so this remains a governance flaw rather than an endorsement of coercive monitoring or a severe safety defect for scoring purposes. The abstract overstates transferability from one small, hydrogeologically specific pilot and does not explain the likely cost, maintenance burden, or technical staffing required for a larger network.
quality_rationale: The proposal is clear, original, socially aware, and unusually specific about field instrumentation, validation events, data governance, and deliverables. Those are substantial merits. However, its central technical promise depends on spatial and depth resolution that the sparse gravity network is unlikely to support, and the abstract does not provide the sensitivity analysis needed to defend that promise. The social evaluation and emergency governance provisions are also underdeveloped. These weaknesses affect feasibility and inference rather than merely presentation, placing the artefact near the middle of the scale despite its strong framing and polished design.
title: The Weight of Water: Community-Governed Quantum Gravimetry for Contested Aquifers
topic: A pilot network of cold-atom gravimeters intended to produce community-governed evidence about groundwater depletion and water-allocation disputes in a fictional drought-prone delta.
